title: Problem 10
markdown:
### Problem
The real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{31}$ lie in the interval $[-5, 13]$, and $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_{31} = 0$. Show that

$$a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \dots + a_{31}^2 \le 2015.$$

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
Let $m = -5$ and $M = 13$, with $N = 31$.
Notice that $-NmM = -31(-5)(13) = 2015$.

For any real number $x \in [m, M]$, the quadratic $(x - m)(M - x) \ge 0$, because $x - m \ge 0$ and $M - x \ge 0$.

Expanding this product:

$$-x^2 + (m + M)x - mM \ge 0 \iff x^2 \le (m + M)x - mM.$$

Applying this inequality to each $a_j \in [-5, 13]$:

$$a_j^2 \le (m + M)a_j - mM.$$

Summing over all $j = 1, 2, \dots, 31$:

$$\sum_{j=1}^{31} a_j^2 \le (m + M)\sum_{j=1}^{31} a_j - 31mM.$$

Since we are given that $\sum_{j=1}^{31} a_j = 0$, the linear term vanishes completely:

$$\sum_{j=1}^{31} a_j^2 \le 0 - 31(-5)(13) = 31 \times 65 = 2015.$$

### Conceptual Explanation
For any $x \in [m, M]$, the inequality $(x - m)(M - x) \ge 0$ expands to $x^2 \le (m + M)x - mM$. Summing over all 31 variables causes the linear term to drop out since $\sum a_j = 0$, leaving $\sum a_j^2 \le -31mM = 2015$.

### Key Technique
Boundary quadratic inequality $(x - m)(M - x) \ge 0$ annihilating linear sums.
